title: Making rivals depend on your system is the secret to America's 300-year winning streak
dek: The Dutch, the British, and the Americans took turns as top dog—not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake everything on their maritime system. Once they can't live without your shipping lanes and markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
why: Walter Mead breaks down America's 300-year winning formula into a five-step strategy, then pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait, and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable framework for judgment, not news-cycle opinion.
who: Founders going global and those in China–US supply chains; engineers studying the Taiwan Strait or drone warfare; investors tracking AI policy risk.

points.h: Unpredictability is a form of power
points.body: ‘Unpredictability’isn't madness—it's a modern power strategy. Mead says post–Cold War US diplomacy leaned on‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’as a pillar of stability. Trump, by contrast, profits from the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age—the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. Clinton, besieged by the Lewinsky scandal, discovered that shame lives only in other people's minds; keep moving forward and the dogs bark, but the caravan passes. Trump scaled that insight to industrial proportions. The cost is borne by the US diplomatic system: when the world's top power itself becomes the unpredictable card, the alliances and rules built on predictability since World War II start to unravel faster and faster.

points.h: The final step of global hegemony is cutting off
points.body: The Anglo-American maritime order won not through any single battle but through a five-step playbook: first, open societies on islands—17th-century Holland tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital flowed in; then global trade—Dutch merchant ships circled the world, and wealth piled up so high that paintings showed Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Step three: while continental powers fought over Silesia inland, you grabbed India and Canada overseas. Step four is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain's colonial blockades, invite everyone in to do business—the British navy fought pirates, and all merchant ships benefited; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after their wars. The final step is the trump card: once the other side can't live without your grain, rubber, and shipping lanes, cut them off—Germany in World War I suddenly found Argentine grain and Malayan rubber gone, and its economy collapsed.

points.h: All of China's efforts are about preventing the umbilical cord from being cut
points.body: Run the same framework over China, and you see Beijing knows exactly where its lifeline is. Mead says that if the mainland blockaded Taiwan, the US could counter-blockade from 100 miles off Taiwan's coast: oil stops coming in, manufactured goods can't sell, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina go void—China's economy would be strangled. He has discussed these scenarios with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and that worry is always there. So China's energy policy must be read side by side: on one hand, building oil reserves so large the outside world is surprised; on the other, ramping up solar and hydro while mining as much coal as possible. It's not schizophrenia—it's the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the vulnerabilities that come from depending on the outside world. He also warns America against retreating into isolationism—agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to sustain themselves.

points.h: Every wave of technological dividends needs new institutions to match
points.body: Mead starts with the ownership society: at America's founding, the land was full of independent farmers who owned their plots. A bridge might be nice, but it would raise my taxes—that trade-off itself was political education. The railroad era paired with the Homestead Act, as the government gave land to railroad companies and farmers, letting a national market grow. In the 20th century, the family farm was replaced by the suburban single-family home, backed by tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth-distribution machine. Today that machine has hit the wall of housing prices: young people can't afford to live near work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. If the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, the usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius—the physical space that technology opens up can support another two generations. But the prerequisite is institutional‘infrastructure’—he coined the term info-structure, meaning the institutional and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courthouses.

points.h: Silicon Valley tilts toward the Tech Hamiltonian camp
points.body: American foreign-policy debates have for centuries been four schools of rhetoric: Hamiltonian—strong government clearing the way for capital; Wilsonian—spreading liberal democracy; Jeffersonian—fearing big government; Jacksonian—isolationist in peacetime, but when hit, fight to the death. The post–Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamiltonian and Wilsonian, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the tent. Mead says the truly notable new species is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s, tech companies loved to say‘we're a global company, Google has no borders, Washington can't touch us’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic stances have shifted too: old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets; Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, even wants employees to be patriotic—selling code to China is shameful, and colleagues will report you. The commercial core is shifting from old multinationals to tech nationalists—that's the underwater current of America's political realignment.

points.h: The more equipment a great power has, the more it fears technological generational shifts
points.body: Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time, at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones that carry mines to blow up tanks; a few months later, progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, where usually only two or three soldiers operate together, and one of the hardest problems is‘how to evacuate the wounded’—you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people out, while a swarm of drones hunts the enemy's attack drones. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be pulled off the front line. The change flips every six months. The irony for America: the power with the most tanks and carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution—existing equipment goes from advantage to moving cost. The Russian Black Sea Fleet has no major battles to fight, yet it's trapped in port by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

points.h: The most important new variable in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
points.body: On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment: Beijing needs a very high probability of success before crossing the threshold—if it fails, the consequences for the initiator are catastrophic. But between‘attack’and‘do nothing’lies a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade—actions that change the facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The truly new variable on the Taiwan chessboard is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japan's independence is over; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, and reshaping national psychology. Historically, Japan has turned fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor in Japan—that is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

points.h: AI actually makes deterrence more credible
points.body: Applying Cold War deterrence logic to the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive conclusion: deterrence succeeds only if the opponent is 100% convinced that‘if I do X, you will inevitably do Y, and you can and will do it.’As long as the decision chain contains a human veto point—‘I might soften when the moment comes’—that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign-policy decisions and handing them to AI turns retaliation into a mechanism that is executable and won't hesitate—deterrence becomes more credible. But that is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilization-ending scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the issue is‘very interesting and a bit confusing,’and he doesn't think an answer has arrived.

terms.def: A new force in US foreign policy that advocates state power clearing the way for tech companies, replacing old free-market multinational capital.
The institutional, legal, and regulatory framework needed for AI to safely land in settings like hospitals and courts—distinct from physical infrastructure.
The American hawkish tradition of staying out of the outside world in peacetime, but when attacked, using overwhelming force to destroy the enemy.
A method of strangling an opponent's trade without direct war, using customs, insurance, and port rules to slowly squeeze.
